status_reason: Surgical decisions on patients need validation beyond a first assessment, and the kidney study is only an in vitro proof of concept, so it cannot be quoted as proof of readiness.
answer: No, the kidney study cannot be quoted as proof that the sensor is ready for live tumour-boundary decisions. It is an in vitro proof of concept on 14 thawed samples from 7 patients, and its authors report very high variance and unacceptable false negatives. A first step is a lab test of NIR on kidney tumour and normal pairs against histology, plus a check whether NIR with MIR ATR adds information.

inline.headline: Test NIR diffuse reflectance on kidney tumour and normal sample pairs in the lab before any surgical use
inline.probe: NIR diffuse-reflection fiber probe on the lab bench
inline.install: Laboratory bench on kidney tissue samples; no installation in the operating theatre at this stage
inline.test_against: Independent histological classification of the same samples
inline.not_final_because: The study used 14 thawed in vitro samples from 7 patients with very high variance, there are no in vivo data, the four-LED set must be adapted to each case, and the approach is limited to samples suitable for ATR if MIR is added.

problems.text: The kidney study is not proof of surgical readiness: it tested two prototypes on 14 in vitro samples from 7 patients, and the authors call it a proof of concept with very high variance and unacceptable false negatives.

The study can be quoted only as an in vitro proof of concept that an LED-based NIR sensor captured tumour-related variance in kidney samples. The surgical scenario is an application concept with no validation data, and neither applies to a different sensor, organ or set-up without new data.
The study used frozen biopsies that were thawed before measurement, and spectra of frozen or thawed tissue can differ from in vivo measurements.
The study used only four NIR LEDs, and the optimal wavelengths and LED set must be adapted to each organ and cancer type, so the proposed sensor cannot be assumed to work for the surgical use.

methods.why: NIR penetrates up to several millimetres and works with fiber probes for online use, and it is the sensor concept under test in the kidney study.

MIR ATR probes give well-defined peaks but reach only very thin layers, and a combined ATR and fluorescence probe has detected tumour boundaries in model tissue; it is limited to ATR-suitable samples.
Fluorimetry is highly sensitive but relies on secondary emission of certain substances, mostly biological, and FAD fluorescence has been measured in tissue.
Raman signals are weak and often masked by fluorescence in organic tissue, so it needs special probe designs.

questions.q: Will validation samples be fresh or frozen and thawed, and which independent reference (histology) will classify them?
questions.why: Thawed samples can differ from in vivo spectra, and the reference must be independent of the sensor.

questions.why: The kidney study used 14 samples from 7 patients, and the variance reported was very high.

experiment.objective: Test whether NIR, and NIR combined with MIR ATR, separate tumour from normal tissue on the same samples, against independent histology.
steps: Agree the target boundary decision and the independent histological reference with the client.
Measure fresh or thawed kidney tumour and normal pairs with a NIR fiber probe at the proposed sensor wavelengths, and record the thawing condition.
Measure the same spots with a combined ATR probe (MIR ATR and fluorescence) to test whether a combined probe gives more separation than NIR alone.
Validate with segmented cross-validation and randomisation tests, and compare each set against the best single method on the same data.
Repeat the test on a larger sample set before any in vivo or surgical step.
references: S03 p.14: segmented cross-validation and randomisation tests when data are limited
S04 p.2: combined ZrO2 ATR head analysing about 2 mm (IR) and 1 mm (fluorescence) at once
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client; none are stated in the enquiry.

pathway.key_features: Not yet identified for kidney tissue; in the cited tissue study, amide I and II bands near 1640 and 1548 cm-1 and FAD fluorescence at 520-530 nm were reported for chicken and liver tissues, not kidney.
pathway.path_reason: Key spectral features and validation data are missing, so the AFS pathway starts with a multi-method lab test.

multispectral.why: NIR probes several millimetres of tissue while MIR ATR reads only thin surface layers, so the two carry complementary information; NIR with IR was reported to help for tumour boundaries.
multispectral.test: Measure the same spots with NIR alone, MIR ATR alone and the combined set, and accept the combination only if it beats the best single method on the same validation data.

assumptions: The proposed sensor uses the same four-LED NIR set as the kidney study.
The surgical target is kidney tumour tissue.
Tumour boundary means the same tumour versus normal classification used in the kidney study.
No validation data exist for the client's own setup.
